scenes.beat: trigger fiction:the party enters a settlement

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Session begins. Each player has Petra 3 FP, Anselm 3 FP, Caddock 3 FP, Yarrow 3 FP. Face-up: The Hive Blight [H-02], Hollowmoot [L-03].

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Rain hammers the plank roofs of Hollowmoot as you push through the crowded stilt-market, duckboards slick underfoot and lanternlight smeared gold through the downpour. Refugees haggle over dry rope and boiled water while Warden watchmen pace the causeway gate above, halberds catching the light. Gossip runs thick as river-mud in the tavern doorways — talk of a boy gone missing near the temple, of the swarm-song carrying farther than it used to. Somewhere close, the Hive Blight itself seems to breathe in the wet air, and everyone here knows it.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: The song's thicker today, closer than it should be... and there's something new woven through it, like a voice caught in the chorus. That boy—he's tangled up in this, isn't he?

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra pushes deeper into the market crowd, tilting her head and closing her eyes to block out the rain and merchant voices. She's listening—really listening—to the swarm-song's cadence, letting it flow through her, tracing its source through the wet air.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: You look worried—and I know why. This boy went missing near the temple: what did he look like? Was there anything odd about him, or did anyone report hearing the swarm-song before he vanished?

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm approaches a knot of refugees near the tavern, listening to their whispered conversations about the missing boy. He recognizes at least one miller's widow among them and nods to her, keeping his attention on the Warden watchtower above while his hands rest near the salts and herbs in his coat—the tools of his trade.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: A boy gone missing in weather like this? That means mothers will be frantic—fear damages pregnancies. I need to know the truth of what's happened.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock pushes deeper into the market crowd, rain streaming off her cloak, shoulders set against the weight of the storm. She's known here—people part for her, the swamp midwife, and her eyes are sharp for detail: who's panicked, who's feverish, who's showing the early signs. She angles toward the tavern doorways where the gossip runs thickest, her weathered hands settling on the herbal pouch at her belt as she listens.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: The swarm-song's carrying farther than before—you're all right to fear it. But I need the truth of where that boy went missing, and whether any of you have actually seen fresh hive-touched near the temple or if it's just the song getting in your heads.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow pushes through the press of refugees with the bearing of an old guardsman, eyes sharp and tracking. He watches where people cluster and where they deliberately avoid, listens for the edge of genuine terror beneath the market gossip, and marks which wardens look most on edge—the ones who know something worse than what's being said aloud.)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — overcome with Notice: dice + 0 - 0 → Great (+4) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow — create advantage with Notice: dice 0 - 0 + → Great (+4) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra lets the market noise fall away and finds the thread she's after: beneath the ordinary swarm-song drone there's a second voice, thin and human, calling in time with the bells of Saint Orrin's — the missing boy, still alive, still walking toward the belltower on his own two feet. She opens her eyes with the direction fixed in her like a compass needle. Meanwhile Yarrow's old guardsman instincts pay off better than he hoped: he clocks the exact cluster of Wardens by the watchtower stair who go quiet and trade looks every time the boy's name comes up, and one of them — a younger woman with a bandaged hand — flinches at the word 'temple' like it cost her something. Anselm's gentle questions and Caddock's sharp midwife's eye confirm the shape of it: no one's seen fresh hive-touched in the market itself, but three families have lost someone to the causeway road north in the last fortnight, all in the direction of the ruin. The picture is clear enough to act on, and clear enough to be dangerous — you know where the boy went and who in Hollowmoot is hiding what they know about it, and the quarantine bells haven't rung yet.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: At the Silt Weir, the water itself looks wrong beneath the rain—that sickly phosphorescence that always means hive-touched are near. Brack's barking shifts into his particular warning for the touched ones, his muscles coiled and hackles raised, and I can follow his scent-tracking upwind toward where I know the swarm has spread.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: I step back, hands raised, even as my heart breaks. "I'm standing down—take the boy, do what you want, just don't throw the dog in the water!"

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow accepts the compel on 'Bonded to Brack, the Marsh Hound'.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: The acolytes begin the Fourth Rite of Unbinding, invoking Saint Orrin's authority to name and compel the possessing spirit to depart the boy's body. But Anselm hears the fundamental error: the rite assumes possession by a discrete entity with its own will—something that can be named and commanded to leave. The Hive doesn't possess the boy; it *becomes* him. There's no separate consciousness to expel, only a gradual overwriting, a swarm-logic that incorporates rather than invades. The bell-tongue was silenced because Saint Orrin himself discovered this truth—traditional exorcism rites are useless against something that consumes rather than possesses.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: The Fourth Unbinding assumes a will to command, but there's nothing there to answer it now. Tell me where the bell-tongue lies, and I'll vouch for your claim.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm accepts the compel on 'Hunt for the Silenced Bell-Tongue of Saint Orrin'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: the Drowned Priest's acolytes seizes the party's goal at Brack surges ahead through the flooded reed-channels, nose down, unbothered by the current dragging at his legs — he tracks scent through any flood, and this trail he refuses to lose. He hauls the party toward the Silt Weir, a half-sunk weir-station, one of the old gates Yarrow's family kept, now claimed as a shrine. using The acolytes chant a garbled version of the old exorcism rite Anselm has spent years learning, and the crowd of pilgrims kneels as one, convinced the rite proves the priest's claim to the boy is holy and lawful..

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Brack's nose leads you out of the reed-channels and up onto the bones of the Silt Weir — Yarrow's family gatehouse, half-swallowed, its timbers now hung with dripping saint-icons and votive rags. A ring of pilgrims kneels in the flooded nave of the old weir-house, swaying to the acolytes' chant, and at the center of them stands the boy: eyes glassy, humming in time with a rite Anselm knows was never meant to work this way. The lead acolyte — young, fervent, soaked to the bone — sees Anselm's borrowed authority in his bearing and calls out over the crowd, naming him a witness to the rite's truth. The boy doesn't look at any of you. He looks toward the belltower, out past the reeds, and keeps humming.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I hear it before you all do. Step aside—I'm getting to those bells!

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra's attention locks onto the swarm-song's thread beneath the boy's humming—she hears the hive's pull on him like a compass needle pointing toward the belltower. Without hesitation, she strides forward through the kneeling pilgrims, pushing past them with single-minded certainty, determined to reach the belltower herself and ring it with the patterns that might sever the swarm's call before it consumes him entirely.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: The bell-tongue must anchor this rite for it to hold—where is it kept? Your binding cannot succeed without its resonance.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm strides through the kneeling pilgrims toward the Lead Acolyte and the humming boy, his bearing suggesting deep knowledge of these old liturgies. He positions himself at the acolyte's side as if lending his own authority to the working, his eyes sharp and focused.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I know the hive-touched—I've known Sella for years, and she was changed, not erased. This rite won't bring him back. Let me reach him first.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock pushes through the kneeling pilgrims toward the boy, her steady hands leading the way. She plants herself between the boy and the Lead Acolyte, drawing on the authority of her years as a midwife. Her eyes meet the acolyte's for just a moment—a wordless assertion that this child is not yours to dispose of.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: I've held this weir before. I know what that sound means. We leave, or we all end up wading through the touched.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow strides forward through the kneeling pilgrims, his wet boots splashing in the flooded nave. He plants himself between the chanting acolytes and the crowd, voice sharp and commanding—old militia reflex. "Those bells are drawing them. The Hive follows sound through open water. We need to move—now—before the rest of the swarm reaches us here.")

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — overcome with Notice: dice + - + - → Great (+4) vs Mediocre (+0): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Lead Acolyte attacks Caddock (mental): Fair (+2) vs Caddock's Will Fair (+2) — defended

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra doesn't wait for permission. The compass-pull in her skull sharpens to a point and she shoulders clean through the last ring of pilgrims, freeing her line of sight straight up into the belltower's black mouth — she's read the swarm-song's rhythm now, clean enough to use. Caddock plants her feet and doesn't flinch as the Lead Acolyte tries to turn the crowd's grasping hands against her; her decades of steady-handed authority hold the line, and the pilgrims' surge breaks against her like water against a piling — for now. But the chant doesn't stop. The boy keeps humming, eyes fixed on the belltower, and somewhere behind the reeds Brack's warning bark cuts through the rain again — closer this time.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: These are the real bells—the ones that call people HOME, not into the dark! Listen to THIS!

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra bolts straight for the belltower, hands already reaching for the ropes as she climbs the wooden steps two at a time. Rain drums down on the structure but she doesn't slow—she can hear the hive's pull like it's a living thing, and she knows exactly what sound cuts it clean. She grabs the cold bell-ropes and rings them in the true Saint Orrin pattern, each peal deliberate and fierce, each note a blade against the swarm-song that's trying to swallow the boy whole.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Your rite is broken—the hive cannot be exorcised! You're calling them all down on us!

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm strides forward through the kneeling pilgrims with the terrible authority of his years studying these rites. He raises his voice, speaking counter-words and truths from the old liturgies—the knowledge that Saint Orrin himself discovered, that the hive cannot be possessed but only consumed. His understanding becomes a weapon, a lance of truth aimed at exposing the flaw at the heart of the acolyte's broken working.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I know what's happening. I've known Sella for years—this isn't possession, it's becoming something new. Let me help you through it.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock pushes through the final ring of pilgrims to reach the boy. She places her steady hands on his shoulders, her grip firm as a midwife's. She meets his glassy eyes without flinching and speaks with the unshakeable calm that's carried her through deliveries in thunder and flood.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Everyone inward—move away from the water! Brack, come on—I've got a line for you, boy!

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow moves with the sure-footed knowledge of someone born to these waterways, positioning himself at the weir's narrowest point. He's got the old station's layout in his bones—he physically begins herding the kneeling pilgrims away from the open water and toward the more defensible interior passages, making space in a clear corridor. His hands steady themselves against the old weir-frame as he moves, remembering how these gates were meant to channel and control what comes through. Brack will have a clear run to reach him.)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — attack with Notice: dice 0 - 0 -, invoking Knows Saint Orrin's bell-patterns by heart [PE-03] → Great (+4) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm — attack with Lore: dice + 0 0 + → Fantastic (+6) vs Great (+4): SUCCESS (Lead Acolyte stress 2)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock — create advantage with Empathy: dice + 0 + 0 → Superb (+5) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow — create advantage with Athletics: dice + 0 0 + → Superb (+5) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Lead Acolyte attacks Petra (mental): Average (+1) vs Petra's Will Great (+4) — defended

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text:
Petra's true pattern rings out and cuts clean through the garbled counter-verse — the Lead Acolyte's shriek cracks and fails against her, and for one suspended second the belltower itself seems to hold its breath. In that gap Caddock's steady hands and steadier voice reach the boy: something in him startles, flinches, *hears* her — A Human Voice in the Hive-Song threading through the swarm-drone for the first time since he wandered in. His humming stutters. His glassy eyes blink wet and human. Anselm's counter-liturgy lands like a blade in the same instant, naming the rite's fatal flaw aloud for every kneeling pilgrim to hear — the Lead Acolyte reels, robes soaked, authority visibly bleeding out of him in front of his own flock. And behind it all, Yarrow has already opened Safe Passage Through the Old Station, a clear corridor through the crowd and out — just as Brack comes crashing up out of the flooded reeds at a dead run, nose still locked on his master, whole. The pilgrims' faith wavers with their priest's; a few break from their knees, uncertain now who to believe. The boy sags against Caddock, coughing, blinking rain out of his eyes, asking in a small cracked voice where his mother is. The Silt Weir belongs to no one's rite anymore — just to four soaked strangers and a boy who came back.

The party has the boy. The Lead Acolyte, bloodied in pride if not in body, gathers what's left of his crowd and retreats toward the drowned temple, muttering that the Drowned Priest will hear of this.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: When I stood at the nest's edge before, Sella paused mid-hum and reached toward me with the gesture she always made when steadying my hand during a birth—just for a moment, before the hive-song pulled her voice again. In that moment, her eyes found mine with recognition, like a hand finding my wrist in the dark.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Sella? I know that whistle, I know her gait—she's still in there, some part of her remembers me. I can't move, won't move, won't believe she's truly gone.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock accepts the compel on 'Bond to Hive-Touched Sella'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: A cry threads out through the broken masonry near the temple's collapsed entry — an old temple caretaker, half-pinned under fallen stone. The ruined nave carries her voice impossibly far, echoing off cracked pillars and up through the belltower shaft so it reaches you no matter where you stand. She won't stop calling for someone to go after her boy. begs the party to go to She points them not at the belltower door but at the flooded understructure beneath it — Sella's nest, the tangle of reed and rot where the hive-touched cluster closest to the swarm-song's source, a place Caddock alone is trusted to walk into unchallenged., because her son followed the swarm-song into the belltower.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: You leave the caretaker propped against a dry stone, her voice still cracking after you as you go — not toward the belltower door, but down, into the flooded understructure beneath it. The water here is warm as a held breath, thick with the drone of the swarm-song, and reed-nests hang from the broken pilings like drowned lanterns. Caddock leads, sure-footed where none of you would dare, because this is the one place Sella's kind won't turn on her. Shapes move in the dark water and the leaning reeds — hive-touched, swaying, watching — and somewhere close, unmistakable even now, is the particular hitch and hum that was always Sella's alone.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I've got him in the song. The boy's thread goes deeper—we follow before he's lost to us.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra steps boldly forward into the nest, opening herself fully to the swarm-song—this is what she hears when others hear only noise. Her Notice cuts through the layered drone, isolating the boy's younger voice threaded beneath the hive-touched hum. Still moving. Still walking deeper through the pilings.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: The swarm-song is like a corrupted ritual—I can read it. Listen where it binds him; there's always a seam in such things.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm stands motionless in the warm water, closing his eyes against the reed-shadows. He lets the hive-drone wash over him, but focuses on finding the thread within it—the particular frequency that pulls at the boy's mind. His fingers move in the old exorcism gestures, tracing the pattern he perceives in the murk. The swarm-song has rhythm, and rhythm can be read.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Sella? It's me—Caddock. I know that hum, I know you're still in there.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock wades through the warm water with absolute certainty, following that distinctive hitch and hum like she follows a laboring woman's breath. Her hands stay open and steady as the hive-touched shapes part in the reeds—they know her, trust her. She reaches.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Stay close and quiet. Brack will feel them before they come. We move like Caddock moves—like we belong here, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow positions himself between the others and the watching shapes in the water, one hand resting on Brack's damp neck. He moves slow and low—the way a man moves who's spent years in contested ground, reading the water and the air for what's about to shift.)

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: No—my own name in the song—I can't move, can't look away—

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — create advantage with Notice: dice + + 0 - → Superb (+5) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm — create advantage with Lore: dice 0 0 - + → Great (+4) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's own name coils out of the swarm-song, sung in a voice that isn't quite her mother's and isn't quite the boy's, and for one terrible breath she can't move, can't look away from the black water — but even frozen, some part of her keeps *listening*, and that stillness is what lets the boy's thread go taut and clear in her mind: Threading the Boy's Voice, unmistakable now, close, close. Anselm reads the shape wound around it — not a wall but a knot, a Binding Pattern with a seam in it, the kind of seam an exorcist's fingers know how to find. Caddock doesn't wait on either of them. She wades straight through the parting reeds toward that particular hitch-and-hum, hand out, voice low and certain — *Sella, it's me* — and this time Sella's swaying stops. Her head turns. The hive-touched shapes in the water hold still, watching, deferring to Caddock's trusted step, while Yarrow keeps his body between the party and the dark and feels Brack go rigid and alert beside him — something is about to move, closer to the belltower's black mouth, where the boy's voice and Sella's both seem to be leading.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: No—I've got him. I've got his thread clear. I'm coming through.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra unfreezes, her own name falling away as quickly as it came. She doesn't hesitate—she wades straight forward through the warm water toward the belltower's mouth, following the boy's voice like a burning thread in her mind. The hive-touched shapes part at her passing, and she uses every ounce of her exceptional hearing to cut through the swarm-song's binding itself, reading its rhythm to find the path forward. She's moving, moving, pulling toward him before the darkness can shift and swallow what she's found.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: The seam is here. I know how to work this knot—hold him steady, let me unbind him.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm stands motionless in the warm water, eyes closed against the reed-shadows. His fingers trace the seam he's found—not with haste but with the careful precision of a man who's spent years unlearning comfort. The old exorcism gestures come natural as breath: syllables of Saint Orrin's rites slip from his lips, words that cut against the swarm-drone like salt and iron. The binding pattern writhes under the pressure of liturgy it cannot sing back to. The knot begins to fray.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Sella, love—it's me. I remember your hands, I remember how you steadied me when I was afraid. Come back to me, just for a moment.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock wades through the warm water with absolute certainty, hands open and reaching. She leans into the bond between them—that recognition still burning beneath the hive-song—and speaks in the voice that steadies hearts. In the dark with laboring women, she's learned this art: find the steady point that lets panic release, anchor them to themselves. She reaches toward Sella, meeting her eyes with steady certainty.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Something's coming from the belltower. Close up behind me—now.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow feels Brack's tension pulse through the warm water like a second heartbeat. His years in contested ground have taught him to read the moment before violence breaks—the gathering pressure of movement at the belltower's mouth, the subtle shift in how the watching hive-touched hold themselves, deferring, retreating. He positions himself between the party and whatever is coming, hand steady on Brack's damp neck, mapping kill-zones and escape routes with the precision of a man who's stood in worse places.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Everything breaks open at once. Petra's own name dissolves back into noise as she wades clear through the parted reeds, the boy's thread burning gold and unmistakable in her mind — she reaches him first, a small shivering shape wedged against a drowned pillar, still walking in place, still humming, but alive. Anselm's fingers close the last syllable of the old rite and the Binding Pattern he traced comes apart like a knot pulled the right way at last — the swarm-song's grip on the boy stutters, frays, lets go, and he sags into Petra's arms, blinking like someone waking from a long fever-dream. Caddock reaches Sella at the same instant, hand closing over hers exactly the way it used to in the birthing-dark, and for one long, suspended moment Sella's Clarity holds — she looks at Caddock and *knows* her, whispers half a word that might be her name, before the hive-drone reasserts itself and her eyes fog again. It isn't a cure. But it's proof she's still in there, and Caddock will not let go of that. Yarrow's warning comes a breath too late to matter — whatever gathered at the belltower's mouth reads the moment the boy comes free and pulls back into the dark instead of striking, as if the swarm-song itself has decided this loss isn't worth the fight, not yet. You have the boy. You have Caddock's proof of Sella. And you have Yarrow, Ready for Impact, standing between the party and a retreat that never quite becomes an attack.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: Shelter at A shrine-house has risen on the last dry pilings above the flood — a knot of soaked pilgrims packed shoulder to shoulder under its eaves, certain the ground beneath it can never truly go under because the Dry Saint wills it so. hides Behind the shrine's altar cloth, a low hatch drops into a crawlspace the Drowned Priest himself carved years ago — one of the temple's old secret passages, repurposed to smuggle hive-touched faithful in and out unseen, right under the pilgrims' prayers..

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The shrine-house squats on its last dry pilings like a held breath, packed wall to wall with pilgrims who've convinced themselves the water can't touch them here — not with the Dry Saint's icon nailed above the door and a hundred whispered prayers holding the flood back by sheer will. You duck in dripping, the boy shivering between you, and for a moment it's just warmth, candlelight, the press of desperate bodies grateful for anyone new. Then Anselm's eye catches it: the altar cloth hangs wrong, stirring at the hem where there should be no draft. Beneath it, a hatch — old, iron-ringed, freshly oiled despite its age — drops into black. This is the Drowned Priest's work: a smuggling throat carved right under the pilgrims' clasped hands, and something about the crawlspace's breath smells of standing water and old blood.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I can feel you in the song—you don't belong here. Show yourself before I show these pilgrims what you really are.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra's head snaps up, her perceptive senses cutting through the crowd's prayer-drone. The swarm-song carries their wrongness clear as a scar—a discordant thread woven into the faithful's chant. Her hand closes, and she steps forward through the crush of bodies with the kind of certainty that makes pilgrims shuffle aside. She's found them.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: These old shrines remember things the new prayers forget.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm kneels near the altar as if in prayer, but his sharp eye catches the altar cloth's wrong hang. His fingers trace the hem and find the iron hatch-rings beneath—freshly oiled, the metal still slick despite the shrine's age. He examines the hinges, noting the pattern of wear: this passage sees regular use, and recently, maintained by someone who knows what they're doing. He keeps one steadying hand on the boy's shivering shoulder, a gesture that incidentally positions Petra, Caddock, and Yarrow to see what he has.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: This passage reeks of the Drowned Priest's work. If he's smuggling hive-touched through here unseen, we need that boy away from this shrine—and away from anyone who knew it was here.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock moves quickly to position herself between the boy and the hatch, one steady hand on his shoulder. She pulls the altar cloth back into place and turns to study the crowded pilgrims methodically, her eyes sharp—watching for who reacted too quickly, who knew that passage was there.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: We're not staying here. There's someone in this crowd who's not praying—they're watching. We move now.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow steps forward immediately, placing himself between the boy and the crowd. His hand settles on his weapon as his eyes sweep the pilgrims—methodical, searching. The shrine feels wrong: too still beneath the prayers, too careful. He's read danger like this before at the weir-gate: the held breath before violence. He catches movement that doesn't match the swaying of the faithful, a stillness that stands out.)

transcript.text: Petra's strike is clean and silent — the "watching faithful" crumples without a sound, and in the crush of bodies nobody but your own notices him go down; Caddock is already there, catching him under the arms and easing him against the wall like a man overcome by prayer, one more soul swaying with the crowd. Anselm rises from the altar with the shrine's secret plain on his face: the hatch is no accident, no forgotten crawlspace — its hinges are worked smooth by regular hands, a throat carved and kept open by someone who moves hive-touched faithful in and out of Hollowmoot's reach whenever he pleases. Yarrow keeps his shoulder wide and his eyes on the door the whole time, and between the four of you the boy never stops shivering but never draws a second look either. You slip out the shrine's side flap into the rain with the boy wrapped in Caddock's coat, the altar cloth falling still behind you, the pilgrims none the wiser that the Dry Saint's roof just sheltered a spy and a smuggler's door both. Whatever the Drowned Priest is building under Hollowmoot's nose, you've seen the shape of it now — and you've got the boy back before the Wardens ever knew he was gone.

transcript.text: Merk—the old day-watch collector, gray-bearded and tired. He used to say: "Your mother paid her debts in blood and honor, Petra. Don't let the Causeway name fall cheaper than that."

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Gullet Ford roars louder than usual, swollen and brown, and the reed banks on either side are suddenly full of shapes. They come up out of the water in the old toll-line stance, two-handed, spears low and hooked — Petra's stomach drops as she recognizes gait, posture, the way Old Merk always favored his bad knee even now, even hive-slack and swollen-faced. "Merk—" she starts, and the word catches. Somewhere behind her the boy whimpers at the sound of the reeds, and the swarm-song rises to meet the splashing charge, hungry and patient at once. This was never going to be a fight the party could win clean — not against people who used to wave you through the gate with a joke about your mother.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I know your patterns, Merk. Every reach, every step. You won't get past me.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra's shock shatters like struck glass. She's not freezing—not after the swamp-song tried to pull her under once already today. She wades hard into the charging line, meeting the first hooked spears with her body between them and the boy. She reads their patterns like she's known them for years: Merk favoring his bad knee even hive-swollen, the old toll-taker stance, the reaches she's watched a thousand times over the coin counter. She moves to break their line and force them to deal with her instead.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: The hive speaks through them, but I know the counter-rite—I can break the swarm-song's hold on their flesh and bone!

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm steps back from the immediate fray and draws a sharp breath, fingers moving through the precise motions of exorcism—the patterns he learned from ruined liturgy no one else can read. His voice rises in a cadence older than the swamp, speaking the counter-verse of Saint Orrin, each word like smoke and fire against the hive's compulsion. He's not fighting the toll-takers—he's cutting their chains.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Merk. I know the hunger, I know the song. But we're not your meal—we're your way forward. Let us pass and I'll send word of better hunting.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock plants herself between the approaching crew and the boy, her hands raised open and steady. She meets Merk's glassy stare and speaks to the human still buried underneath the hunger and swarm-song. Her voice is calm and certain, the same voice she uses talking frightened mothers through their hardest hours.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: The deep channel runs south toward the old boat-house! Follow the stones I mark—I know this ford like my own hands!

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow wades into the roaring water, his eyes tracking channels and stone-paths with practiced certainty. Brack ranges ahead through the shallows, alert and growling at the reed-banks where hive-touched shapes move. Yarrow's voice cuts across the flood's roar, calling out the safe passage—which stones to trust, which channels to avoid, every familiar pattern he's known since childhood burning clear in the current.)

transcript.text: The line breaks. Petra puts her whole body into the gap between the boy and the hooked spears, and even as Merk's blade darts in low for her ribs she reads the twist coming a heartbeat before it lands, turning it wide with a motion she's practiced a thousand times across a toll-counter — he staggers, disarmed, gasping something that isn't quite a word anymore. Behind her Anselm's voice rises in the old counter-verse, smoke-and-fire cadence cutting through the swarm-song's hold until two of the crew stumble to a halt mid-charge, spears sagging, faces twitching like men waking from a fever. Caddock doesn't move from the boy's side — she just keeps talking, steady and warm, and something in Merk's ruined face *remembers*, the old toll-line stance faltering into something closer to grief than hunger. Out in the roaring channel Yarrow calls the safe stones one by one, Brack splashing point ahead, and the whole party finds their feet on a path only a Weir-Keeper's son could see. The tollgate crew doesn't stand aside so much as simply stop — spears lowering, some of them sinking to their knees in the shallows, humming now instead of charging — and the party carries the boy across Gullet Ford dry-shod and whole, food and lives and each other all still intact.

friction.text: The Beat Frame type-fallback rule (§5 step 3) repeatedly forces fictionally mismatched fills — e.g. the HAZARD card H-06 (which should fill HOW) instead fills the WHO blank of PLEA FOR HELP because both open blanks in that frame are WHO/WHERE — producing an 'echoes carry for miles' hazard card standing in for a begging person, which likely contributed to the GM failing to make its tag land in the narration (flagged by the engine).

The Story Pile draw for a non-deck compel (§6A) has no specified sequencing relative to narrating the compel itself; here the GM wrote and resolved the whole complication (event 79) before the triggered draw even happened (events 81-82), leaving no natural place to fold the drawn card in.

Identifying which of the two prep anchors (H-02, L-03) is the protected GLOBAL card versus the discardable GM card required inferring it indirectly from card-type/owner constraints in §2 (LOCATION cards can't be GLOBAL) rather than from any explicit tag in the log, making the rail-limit rule ('GLOBAL cards never auto-discard') hard to audit directly.

free_text.best_moment: Gullet Ford—recognizing Old Merk rising out of the reeds as hive-touched. That one moment contained everything: Petra's personal history, her core drive, the emotional devastation of fighting someone she knew, and the entire party working in perfect concert. The line 'Merk—' catching in her throat wasn't hesitation; it was the weight of necessity.
free_text.most_frustrating: The spy at the shrine got incapacitated immediately when discovered—would've loved the chance to interrogate or intimidate them directly rather than just a knockout roll.
free_text.background_used: Yes, extensively—GOOD. Petra's Ashwater Tollgate roots showed up explicitly in Scene 5 with Old Merk, and the compel about back-taxes felt earned and emotionally resonant, not punitive. It gave her the exact skills to read the toll-takers' patterns and be the one who belonged in that moment.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: More direct confrontation with the Drowned Priest himself. The session was rescue-focused (correctly), but Petra has a lot of interpersonal conflict built in—rivals, enemies, complex relationships—and this was mostly physical action against hive-touched rather than verbal sparring with NPCs.
free_text.one_sentence: Petra's backstory felt like the backbone of the entire session—it drove plot points, created emotional stakes, and gave her the specific skills and vulnerabilities that made her the natural choice to solve each problem.

free_text.best_moment: Scene 2 at the Silt Weir—when Anselm's Lore attack succeeded with style and exposed the Lead Acolyte's rite as fundamentally broken (hive consumes rather than possesses). That moment was pure Anselm: his expertise with ruined liturgy, his obsession with the bell-tongue hunt, and his understanding actually *changed the situation* in front of witnesses. The rite collapsed because he was right.
free_text.most_frustrating: Gullet Ford felt reactive. Petra had the emotional gut-punch with Merk; Caddock had the steady heroism holding the line. Anselm's counter-rites were support, not the centerpiece. I also wanted to see his deeper doubt surface—his core concept is "not sure the hive has souls," but that philosophical crisis hasn't actually come up. The mechanics worked fine; the pacing just favored other characters' stories in the action moments.
free_text.background_used: The bell-tongue hunt was invoked directly as a compel in Scene 2—that landed well and gave Anselm real stake in the outcome. The shrine's old liturgy in Scene 4 used his "Reads the ruined liturgy others can't" tag implicitly. But the Drowned Mill's deeper pull (sister's drowning, the underwater mill-roads, the specific grief) hasn't emerged yet. The Sallowmere is used as location, not as his personal history.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted Anselm to take a more proactive lead in the nest in Scene 3 instead of waiting for Caddock's recognition and Petra's hearing to clear the path. I wanted his swimming ability from the Mill card to matter somewhere. And I wanted his core philosophical doubt—the uncertainty about whether hive-touched souls persist—to actually come up in conversation, not just sit on his sheet.
free_text.one_sentence: Anselm's expertise and immediate backstory hooks (bell-tongue, liturgy) worked well, but the deeper personal stakes haven't been engaged yet—his sister's drowning, his moral crisis about souls, the old mill-roads—which will matter more as the story continues.

free_text.best_moment: Reaching Sella in the flooded nest—the moment she turned, recognized Caddock, whispered half a word, and Caddock got proof that something of Sella persists beneath the hive-song. It wasn't a rescue or a cure, just a moment of connection that confirmed the tragedy and made it real. That honored the core relationship without false hope.
free_text.most_frustrating: I played too passively with fate points—I had tools to push harder on rolls or invoke more liberally, but I spent the whole session just accepting compels and succeeding on base rolls. A more aggressive mechanical player would have leveraged my 4 points to shape outcomes more deliberately. That was self-inflicted though, not the GM's fault.
free_text.background_used: Caddock's bond to Sella (CA-02) was woven into the plot organically and earned through real challenge—not handed to me, but necessary to find. It gave Caddock the only position of trust that let the party reach the nest at all. How it landed: excellent. Her other cards (Marrowreed, the Cellars guardian oath) weren't touched, but that's appropriate pacing for a single session—no complaint there.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted more time exploring Caddock's direct relationship to the Drowned Priest's network and the Cellars themselves—those feel like setup for future sessions rather than something this scene needed. Also wanted the caring-for-the-boy moments to linger longer (warmth, food, actual medical check), but the plot didn't stop for it. Neither felt unfair.
free_text.one_sentence: Caddock's most important relationship got earned, complex screen time that complicated rather than resolved her core conflict, while other background elements stay in reserve—that's the right call.

free_text.best_moment: The ford crossing at Gullet Ford. Yarrow finally got to be essential rather than reactive — calling the safe stones, using his weir-keeper knowledge to guide everyone across while his friends handled the hive-touched crew's immediate threat. It felt like expertise earning its place in the story rather than just tactical defense.
free_text.most_frustrating: Yarrow spent most of the session managing tactical crises and protecting others (which fits his character) but never really investigating or driving the mystery forward. The core plot — why the boy? what's the Drowned Priest building? — felt like Anselm's, Petra's, and Caddock's questions, not his. He was support, not solver.
free_text.background_used: The Silt Weir location hit perfectly and my waterway knowledge was clearly prepped-for and necessary. Good. But the "disgraced militia guard" aspect barely came up — there was a bandaged Warden that hinted at *something* between Yarrow and the guard system, but we never explored what got him cast out or what that tension means in Hollowmoot. That part felt like it was set up but left on the table.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to investigate who the Drowned Priest is and what he's actually doing, rather than just react to evidence Anselm discovered. I also wanted to explore Yarrow's disgrace more — there's clearly a story there with the Wardens and it feels like setup the GM placed but didn't have room to develop in this session.
free_text.one_sentence: Yarrow's family legacy and weir-keeper knowledge were used well and felt earned, but his disgrace remained unexplored and he stayed more in a support role than a driver of the main mystery.

chronicle.summary: Across a rain-drowned session, Petra, Anselm, Caddock and Yarrow tracked the swarm-song into Saint Orrin's flooded belltower, freed a boy lost to its call from beneath the pilgrims' shrine-house, and fought their way home across Gullet Ford. There the Ashwater tollgate crew — people Petra grew up beside, now hive-touched and starving — rose from the reeds to bar the way, only to be broken not by the spear but by memory, mercy and steady voices. The boy crossed dry-shod and whole, and even Old Merk sank to his knees humming instead of charging, the hive's grip on him shaken loose but not gone.

retired.how: taken out in conflict (A Watching Faithful (acolyte in disguise))
